subject: AI & Agents
title: The Black Box Problem
description: A 60-second lesson on The Black Box Problem.

hook.text: A loan application is denied. The bank says 'the algorithm decided.' Nobody can explain why.

buildup.text: Many AI models are black boxes — they produce outputs but can't explain their reasoning.

discovery.text: Explainable AI (XAI) techniques try to reveal which factors most influenced a decision.

twist.text: Simpler models are more explainable but less accurate. There's a trade-off.

climax.text: Regulations now require explanations for automated decisions that affect people's lives.

punchline.text: If you can't explain it, should you deploy it?

quiz.question: What is the black box problem in AI?
options: Models produce decisions without explainable reasoning
Users can't see the computer running the model

details.summary: Many AI systems make decisions through processes too complex for humans to interpret. This black box problem makes it difficult to understand why an AI reached a specific conclusion or recommendation.
details.whyItMatters: When people cannot understand an AI's reasoning, they cannot challenge unfair outcomes. Explainability is essential for trust, accountability, and informed consent.
takeaways: Complex AI models make decisions humans cannot easily interpret
The black box problem hinders accountability and trust
Explainable AI research aims to make models more transparent

faq.question: Why are many AI systems considered black boxes?
faq.answer: Deep neural networks contain millions or billions of parameters interacting in complex ways. Even the developers often cannot trace exactly why the model produced a specific output.

faq.question: What is explainable AI and how does it help?
faq.answer: Explainable AI techniques like LIME and SHAP provide approximations of why a model made a decision. While imperfect, they offer some transparency for users affected by AI choices.
